extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing stand-up comedians; students of Greg Dean's classes
extracted.subtask_description: A glossary-style instructional guide to the techniques, structures, roles, and production standards for writing and performing stand-up comedy using Greg Dean's methods (joke structure, Joke Prospector, storytelling POVs, stagecraft, and material management).

rubrics_metrics.name: 1st Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in audience's minds based upon receiving a joke's Setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one of the five joke structure mechanisms that connect Setup and Punchline; teaches writers to create a vivid mental scene with the setup so the audience builds the Target Assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2nd Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in audience's minds based upon receiving a joke's Punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts as the punchline's mental scene that makes the joke make sense; paired with 1st Story to control audience imagery across Setup and Punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3 POVs (Narrator / Self / Character POV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of View used in storytelling where the comedian adopts performance roles during routine: Narrator POV, Self POV, and Character POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians should learn to shift among the three POVs in storytelling; Narrator POV tells the story, Self/Character POVs are used when acting out scenes (see Anatomy of Funny Storytelling).

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 joke mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In Greg Dean's model the five mechanisms connecting Setup and Punchline are: 1st Story, Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation, and 2nd Story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this model (and the joke diagram) to diagnose why a joke works or fails and to systematically write one-liners and punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connector
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke structure mechanism at the center of all comedy, defined as 1 thing with at least 2 interpretations (ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Connector is the pivot of misdirection; craft connectors that naturally support both the expected (Target Assumption) and the unexpected (Reinterpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target Assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The expected interpretation of the Connector, established by the Setup to misdirect the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setups should create a believable Target Assumption so the Reinterpretation (punchline) surprises and produces laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The unexpected interpretation of the Connector expressed in the Punchline that shatters the Target Assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write punchlines that are compatible with the Connector but unexpectedly reinterpret it; the contrast between Target and Reinterpretation produces surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: joke / joke structure (Setup, Punchline, Tag)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is a single unit of humor of two sections: Setup and Punchline (sometimes with Tag). Setup establishes the Target Assumption; Punchline communicates the Reinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and map Setup → Connector → Punchline (and optional Tag) when writing; use tags to extend laughs without new setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: TCR (Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for the core three elements of Greg Dean's joke structure: Target Assumption, Connector, and Reinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TCR as a checklist when crafting or editing jokes to ensure the mechanism of misdirection is present and clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Prospector Writing System (Joke Map + Joke Mine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-part joke writing system: the Joke Map (topic→punch-premise→setup-premise→setups) and the Joke Mine (turning setups into punchlines using the five mechanisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the step-by-step process to produce one-liners from a topic; the system is taught as a scaffolded method for consistent joke generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Map
rubrics_metrics.description: First part of the Joke Prospector: starts with a topic, creates a punch-premise and setup-premise, and concludes with writing a series of setups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Joke Map to focus and generate multiple setups from a single topic/premise before mining for punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Mine
rubrics_metrics.description: Second part of the Joke Prospector: uses setups from the Joke Map and applies the five mechanisms (Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation) to write punchlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically mine many possible Reinterpretations for a given Connector to find the strongest punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup-Premise / Punch-Premise / Routine Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Premise defined as the message of jokes/routines; setup-premise is a step producing setups and is opposite the punch-premise (Greg Dean: statement with a negative opinion used to write jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate clear premises to direct material so setups and punchlines align around a coherent comedic position.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 LPMs (Laughs Per Minute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for Laughs Per Minute. 5 or more laughs per minute is the professional standard for stand-up comedy shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for ≥5 LPMs as a professional benchmark; use LPM to measure and pace routines and to evaluate material's density and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABCs material rating system
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating system that assigns values to jokes within routines (and routines within shows) with A being the funniest, B second-best, and C weakest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ABCs to inventory and rank material; plan set order using BCAs (place B first, C middle, A to close).

rubrics_metrics.name: BCAs (Material ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective order for placing jokes within routines or routines within shows: B material first, C material in the middle, and A material to close the routine or show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure shows so energy builds to the strongest material; use BCAs to avoid fading and to finish on top.

rubrics_metrics.name: hammock
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique of placing weak or new material between two strong jokes or routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hammock to protect experimental or weak material by surrounding it with proven jokes (see BCAs, sandwich).

rubrics_metrics.name: graph (evaluating jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual device with dots used for evaluating the effectiveness of jokes to determine their placement within routines or shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot audience responses to identify best/worst jokes and inform ABC ratings and show order.

rubrics_metrics.name: joke file / gag file
rubrics_metrics.description: An organized collection of jokes and routines kept on index cards or digitally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a joke/gag file over time to track what works, test variations, and find tags/callbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: set / set list / show list
rubrics_metrics.description: Set: routines or shows of any length and also the act of repeating material consistently. Set list / show list: bullet-point reminders of the order of jokes or routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a set list to rehearse and run shows consistently; ensure repetition preserves delivery, timing, and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: closer / capper / closing line
rubrics_metrics.description: Final joke or routine designed to get a huge laugh while the comedian exits; closer often the strongest material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with A material; plan a capper that leaves audience on a high note and reinforces the show's arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: opener / feature / headliner (show roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional show lineup roles (opener, feature/middle, headliner/closer) with defined time lengths and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare appropriate length routines (3-5, 10, 30, 45–60 minutes) and tailor material/energy to the role you're booked for.

rubrics_metrics.name: stage time
rubrics_metrics.description: What comedians need in front of audiences to gain experience; also the duration (in minutes) comedians get to perform at a show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek regular stage time to refine timing, delivery, and material; use stage time goals to build 3-5, 10, and longer routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: timing / comic timing / comedy timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tempo, rhythm, and emphasis of material and response in a feedback loop that develops between comedian and audience during performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice pauses, beats, and rhythm; timing is central to landing punchlines and managing audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Style of intonation, inflection, pace, timing, and character idiosyncrasies in presenting comedy material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a delivery that complements the joke's setup and punchline; delivery errors can kill otherwise strong material.

rubrics_metrics.name: take a beat / pause
rubrics_metrics.description: Pause or break during a show for delivery and comic timing often between Setup and Punchline or after a Punchline to let the audience laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pauses to allow laughter and processing; don't hurry a joke or talk over laughs (see stay in the bit, step on laughs).

rubrics_metrics.name: stay in the bit
rubrics_metrics.description: After a Punchline during audience laughter, stop talking and remain in the same emotion or state to give the audience permission and space to laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to keep momentum and preserve laughs; avoid stepping on laughs or revealing the joke's mechanism immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: step on laughs / talk over laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: After delivering a Punchline, continuing to speak or take overt action that causes the audience to stop laughing (negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid this anti-pattern; respect audience laughter and time it to maximize LPM and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: hurry a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating a joke faster than the audience can comprehend the Setup–Punchline relationship, which can diminish or kill the laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow processing time; pace delivery to match audience processing rather than the performer's anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: telegraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Causing the audience to guess the Punchline before it's delivered—Setup has too much information or an acting choice reveals the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim setups and acting choices that prematurely reveal the Reinterpretation; preserve misdirection.

rubrics_metrics.name: talking head (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics who memorize words and deliver them with no emotion or physical movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid static delivery; integrate physicality, character, and dynamic vocal choices to engage the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: act out / scene work / storytelling with scene work
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene work where the comedian portrays narrators and characters (Self/Character POV) and acts out all roles within stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use acting, staging, tenses, and POV shifts to make storytelling jokes vivid; contrast with storytelling without scene work (Narrator only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomy of Funny Storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Greg Dean’s model of three performance roles (Narrator, Self, Character POV) used in stand-up storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to distribute setup/punch/tag across POVs and to shift POVs smoothly during story jokes for maximum effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: improv / ad-lib / crowd work
rubrics_metrics.description: Spontaneous jokes and banter with the audience; crowd work uses audience questions to find laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop ad-lib and improvisational skills to handle unexpected situations, stretch, and to warm up or tailor shows; prepare heckler lines and comebacks for interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: heckler lines / comebacks / shut down
rubrics_metrics.description: Insult jokes or quick replies prepared to address hecklers and put them down while restoring control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and memorize a set of heckler lines suitable for different heckler types; use them to regain rhythm without derailing the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: housekeeping (MC duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties of the MC to make announcements, promote shows, recognize birthdays, point out exits, calm hecklers, sell merchandise, run raffles, and end shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MCs should balance housekeeping with humor; it's a functional role that sets tone and keeps the show running smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: tailor (material to audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting or altering material to fit a unique performing situation and different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust references, examples, and tone to match audience demographics and event context; avoid inside jokes that exclude the room (see common knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: clean material / blue material / x-rated material
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories of material defined by suitability for broadcast/network TV: clean (no curse words), blue (graphic sexual/scatological language), x-rated (very offensive content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material appropriate to venue and audience expectations; be aware that blue/x-rated material may be unacceptable in many professional settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: edgy / hurt line (risk boundary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edgy material deals with hurtful subjects but maintains comedic tone; hurt line is the tipping point where comedy becomes real pain and crosses into drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and respect the hurt line; edgy can work if controlled, but crossing into true hurt can derail a set and alienate audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: hack / hacky / comic's clichés (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing overused, clichéd topics and lines with exaggerated delivery betrays a lack of original thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hacky material and clichés; strive for fresh premises and original connections. Use the ABCs to weed out hacky jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: graphology of show roles (avails / availability / booking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical standards for booking: prepare 3-5 and 10 minute routines and availability calendars (avails) to send to bookers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have polished, time-specific sets ready on request and communicate avails professionally to bookers.

rubrics_metrics.name: rehearsal process / improper rehearsal / self talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehearsal method note: improper rehearsal (repeating only words aloud) can cause performer to rely on internal 'self talk' cues, harming natural delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice with emotion, movement, and audience simulation to encode performance in behavior rather than rote words; rehearse presence as well as lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: warm up (personal & audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions before shows: physical warmups, ritual play, run set order, create entrance jokes; also warm up the room at beginning of show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use warm-up routines for confidence and to prepare the audience; early crowd work can unify the room for better responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: graphical and filing tools for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphs and files (joke file, gag file) plus recorded video reviews to evaluate and improve jokes, placement, and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and review showcases; use video review services and iterative filing to refine ABC ratings and show structure.
